newsitem.title: UK: Too late for bid to bring UK'S Major down - Unionist.
newsitem.headline: Too late for bid to bring UK'S Major down - Unionist.

text.p: The time has past for parliamentary manoeuvres to force Prime Minister John Major into an early British election, the leader of the Northern Ireland party whose support would be essential for such an attempt said on Thursday.

David Trimble, whose nine Ulster Unionists effectively hold the balance of power in the House of Commons, told journalists: "Timing (of an election) now is not significant. There are only two or three weeks between the possible dates."
Major, whose Conservatives are 21 points behind the opposition Labour Party in the latest opinion poll, is believed to want to hold an election on May 1.

But speculation has been rife in parliamentary circles that Labour might put down a motion of no confidence in the government if it wins a parliamentary by-election being held on Thursday in an attempt to force a poll on April 10.
A Labour victory in the Wirral South poll would mean the combined forces of all the opposition parties would have one more seat in the Commons than the Conservatives.
But Trimble, whose party is seen as Major's most likely source of outside support, said he had not been approached by Labour about any plan for such a motion.
"I am sure Labour will want to stage some sort of demonstration after the (Wirral) result, but I don't get the feeling that Labour will be going all out to bring the government down early," he said.
Trimble said the Ulster Unionists had managed to secure a number of policy advances in recent weeks, but denied that they were being "bought off" by the Conservatives.

He said the government had agreed to extend local council tax relief for village shops in Northern Ireland, and had made it clear to Brussels that Northern Irish should have priority in the lifting of the export ban on British beef.

Trimble said he expected a further advance shortly in the shape of an extension of the powers of parliament's Northern Ireland Grand Committee to consider non-contentious legislation affecting the province.
"I regard these as things which ought to have happened anyway," Trimble said. "We don't regard ourselves as being bought off."

Asked whether he personally was closer to the Conservatives than to Labour, Trimble said the policy differences between the two parties were now very narrow. "We have to work with whoever is in power," he said.
